Maladaptive Strategies.value: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself

Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

Negative Appraisals.value: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

vignette:
Arthur, at 73, was a man whose life had been built on observation. As a photojournalist, he had spent five decades framing the world, finding order in chaos, and telling stories through a lens. Now, his own story felt incoherent, a chaotic loop playing in the confines of his small apartment. It had been eighteen months since the hotel explosion, and the world he once navigated with confidence had become a landscape of potential threats.

He had been on assignment, covering a mundane press conference on urban renewal in the grand atrium of the St. Regis. Mid-sentence, the world dissolved into a concussive roar. A gas main had ruptured in the basement. He remembered the sudden, absolute unpredictability of it all—the feeling of the floor dropping away, the air thickening with a fine, choking powder. The most visceral memory was the taste, a gritty paste of pulverized concrete and drywall that coated his tongue and throat. By sheer, dumb instinct, his hands had tightened on his camera, and he had captured the skeletal remains of the atrium, images that would later win him a final, bitter award.

In the months that followed, the event refused to stay in the past. The memory would unspool without warning, not as a recollection but as a raw, sensory replay. He would be trying to read the morning paper and suddenly feel the floor shake, the roar filling his ears as if it were happening right now. When the intrusive images were particularly intense, he found the only way to silence them was to immediately go online and buy something, the focus on the transaction providing a brief, powerful distraction. This constant reliving of the event (Memory) convinced him that the danger was not over, that he could never truly be safe, leaving him in a state of perpetual, exhausting vigilance (Threat). The sheer horror of these flashbacks also cemented a core belief: that he was permanently broken and would never feel normal emotions again (Negative Appraisals). The intensity of the memories (Memory) made even the idea of unpredictability a potent source of fear, sensitizing him to new triggers (Triggers).

His inability to relax (Threat) became a defining feature of his existence. At night, he would lie awake for hours, listening for the faintest sound that might signal an intruder, his body rigid with tension. This hypervigilance (Threat) often served as the cue for the memory film to start rolling again, pulling him back into the dust and chaos (Memory). This constant feeling of being hunted convinced him that his life had lost all meaning, that he was just waiting for the next disaster (Negative Appraisals). Because he was always on alert (Threat), he became acutely aware of potential triggers in his environment, seeing imminent danger in a news report about a fire or a sudden shout on the street (Triggers).

Arthur came to believe that thinking about the event was itself a danger. If he let the thoughts in, he was certain he would not be able to handle it (Negative Appraisals). This desperate mental avoidance had the paradoxical effect of making the memories feel even more alien and fragmented when they inevitably broke through, so extreme that it was hard to believe they had actually happened to him (Memory). His conviction that life was now meaningless (Negative Appraisals) created a profound void that he tried to fill with impulsive purchases. A new watch, a first-edition book, an expensive camera lens he didn’t need—these things offered a fleeting distraction, a momentary sense of control over something, anything (Maladaptive Strategies).

His world shrank as he organized it around managing the threat. In the rare times he met his son for lunch, he would arrive early to secure a table where he could sit with his back against a wall, his eyes constantly scanning the entrance and noting any object that could be used as a weapon. This behavior (Maladaptive Strategies), meant to create safety, instead kept his nervous system on high alert, reinforcing his sense of imminent threat (Threat). Seeing a photo of a collapsed building online (Trigger) could send him into a fugue state where he would freeze completely, sometimes for a full minute on a busy sidewalk (Maladaptive Strategies). The shame following these episodes, or after a compulsive spending spree (Maladaptive Strategies), would deepen his conviction that his life was meaningless and out of control (Negative Appraisals). The act of constantly scanning his environment (Maladaptive Strategies) also made him more likely to spot potential triggers, locking him further into the cycle (Triggers).

He finally sought help after an incident at the supermarket last week. A pallet of canned goods was dropped, the crash echoing through the aisles. The sudden, unpredictable noise (Trigger) plunged him into a full-bodied flashback. He froze, dropping his basket, the phantom taste of dust filling his mouth as he felt, with absolute certainty, that the ceiling was coming down. When he came to, a young store employee was asking if he was alright, and Arthur saw the pity in the man’s eyes. It was the moment he realized his strategies weren't keeping him safe; they were keeping him imprisoned. He came to therapy because the meaning he’d lost was not just in the world, but in himself, and he wanted, more than anything, to find a way to live in the present without it being constantly devoured by the past. Each sudden noise or alarming headline served as fresh evidence for his growing conviction that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that his life within it was now meaningless. The only way he found to manage this pervasive sense of danger was to shrink his world, systematically eliminating places and situations he couldn't fully control, starting with the busy downtown cafes he once frequented.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not describe how external triggers directly reinforce the patient's negative beliefs about himself or the world.
The vignette does not describe how the trauma memory itself directly leads to the use of a maladaptive coping strategy.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not describe how external triggers directly reinforce the patient's negative beliefs about himself or the world.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not describe how the trauma memory itself directly leads to the use of a maladaptive coping strategy.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
